extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, government attorneys, and administrative law practitioners (those advising on appropriations, Army regulations, and service disability/pension questions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal principles for construing statutes and Army regulations, and for determining military 'line of duty' questions (including pension/compensation consequences). Targets interpretation of permissive/mandatory language, the effect of regulations, and factual rules for service injuries/disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'may' in appropriation acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an appropriation act provides that so much of a sum 'as may be necessary' may be expended for a public work, the word 'may' is generally to be construed to mean that so much of the appropriation as may be necessary shall be expended; it is not to be assumed from the use of 'may' alone that the duty to expend is discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In appropriation acts for public benefit and works, do not infer a discretion to do or not do the work from the mere use of 'may' unless a modifying clause indicates otherwise. (C. 2^73, July, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'authorized' may be mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'authorized' often confers discretion, where the statute plainly contemplates that an action should be taken the word 'authorized' should be construed as mandatory (i.e., 'directed' or 'required').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include authority to issue commissions dated prior to an existing commission, to issue duplicate discharge certificates, or to sell portions of reservations where Congress evidently intended the action to be performed. (P. 58, Mar., 1893; P. 36, Nov., 1889; R. 27, Feb., 1869.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with prescribed mode and form is condition precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute clearly requires an act to be done in a particular mode or form, the performance cannot legally be materially varied by the officer charged with it; compliance with the prescribed plan/mode is a condition to proper expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an appropriation specifying erection of a bridge 'according to a certain designated plan' makes construction according to that plan a condition to expenditure. (R. 28, June, 1869.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of time from an act excludes that day
rubrics_metrics.description: Where time is to be computed from an act done, the day on which the act is done is to be excluded unless the statute prescribes otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule in statutory time computation. (G. 108^, Mar. 2, 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension act can revive a lapsed authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A later act that extends the time for commencing work, without reenacting the prior act, may have the effect of reviving the earlier authority that had become inoperative by lapse of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: authority to bridge navigable waters that ceased if work not commenced within two years was considered revived by an act extending the time. (P. 59, Apr., 1893.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation acts do not implicitly repeal separate statutory advertising requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions in appropriation acts concerning purchasing do not necessarily repeal or supersede distinct statutory provisions requiring certain statements in advertisements (e.g., preference to domestic products) because the appropriation language relates only to purchasing, not advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3716 (advertising preference) remains operative despite later purchasing provisions in appropriation acts. (P. 60, June, 1892.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited use of legislative debates in statutory construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks of members of Congress in debate do not ordinarily constitute a safe basis for accurately construing an enacted statute; they may be resorted to to ascertain the general object or mischief the legislation sought to remedy when members concurred, but are of little use where members expressed differing views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative debate is admissible only cautiously and generally only to illuminate purpose, not to define terms. (R. 37, June, 1876; opinions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Penal provisions construed narrowly
rubrics_metrics.description: In applying penal provisions (e.g., Articles of War) to particular cases, a case should not be treated as within the penal provision unless it is quite clearly included by the words of description employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penal statutes are to be strictly construed. (R. 37, July, 1876; C. 158U, Jan. 21, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations include necessary incidental authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation for a particular purpose generally includes authority to make the necessary incidental acts required to accomplish that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: appropriation to light arc lights included authority to excavate and extend underground conduits to carry current. (C. 4641, July 30, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso may be substantive and permanent legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proviso appearing in an appropriation act may, in substance, be an independent, general, and permanent provision rather than a mere limitation on the appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a purchase provision framed as a proviso was held to constitute general and permanent legislation even though later appropriation acts omitted that language. (P. 4 159, Aug. 2, 1884.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Army Regulations and differing legal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations fall into three classes: (1) those sanctioned/confirmed by Congress, (2) those made pursuant to and in execution of a statute, and (3) those made by the President as Commander in Chief; each class has distinct legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class (1): Congressional approval as 'regulations' generally adds nothing to statutory effect. Class (2): have force of law while operative but remain subject to Executive modification/waiver. Class (3): are executive/administrative and subject to Executive change. (R. 39, Oct. 23, 1877; C. 29295, Dec. 7, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations conflicting with statutes are inoperative
rubrics_metrics.description: An Army regulation that conflicts with an existing act of Congress has no legal effect; if an act of Congress subsequently conflicts with a regulation, the regulation becomes inoperative to the extent of the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations are subordinate to statute law; numerous decisions cited. (R. 28, 255; multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive may modify or waive regulations subject to law and vested rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations made pursuant to statute are subject to the authority of the Executive to modify them from time to time or to waive their operation in particular cases, provided such changes do not violate statutory law or encroach upon vested contractual rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Secretary of War dispensed with contractor bond required by regulations where government interests demanded; but one may not abrogate statutory or vested rights by waiver. (C. 2074, Mar., 1896; IX Comp. Dec. 280, 284.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations cannot confer powers reserved to legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: An authority which can legally be vested only by legislation cannot be conferred by executive regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: directing expenditure of proceeds from sale of prisoners' manufactured articles (public funds) could not properly be the subject of an Army regulation. (R. 42, Oct., 1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations should not attempt to legislate on subjects occupied by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: It is at least of doubtful validity for executive regulations, even in furtherance of statutes, to be construed so as to extend to subjects the control of which the Constitution expressly vests in Congress but on which Congress has failed to legislate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exercises of power are constitutionally questionable and should be avoided. (C. H749, June 1, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations are not retroactive unless clearly so expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations, like statutes, are not to be given retroactive effect unless the language used clearly requires retroactive operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General presumption against retroactivity. (P. 28, Nov., 1888.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations promulgated through Secretary are acts of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations promulgated through the Secretary of War are to be received as acts of the Executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include United States v. Eliason and others. This character affects their relation to statute law. (Multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that diseases/injuries are in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Per circular (Surgeon General's Office, May 11, 1893), it is just to assume that diseases contracted or injuries received while an officer or soldier is in the military service occur in the line of duty unless the surgeon knows: (1) the disease/injury existed before entering service; (2) it was contracted while absent from duty on furlough or otherwise; or (3) it occurred due to willful neglect or immoral conduct of the sick man himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption governs surgical/medical marks and initial findings unless contrary knowledge exists. (C. 2474, Aug. 3, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and factual determination by commander and surgeon
rubrics_metrics.description: In alleged disability cases the company commander and post surgeon must investigate the circumstances and determine whether the disability was incurred in line of duty; their determinations of fact are ordinarily conclusive when the man has been accorded a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should record facts and remember that their opinions are evidence which is usually conclusive. (C. 13077, Aug. 26, 1892; 17202, Dec. 1, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability may be outside line even if not misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A disability, though not caused by misconduct, may nevertheless be caused by something outside the line of duty (example given: loss of life while attempting to save another's life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case must be considered on its facts; non-misconduct does not automatically imply in-line status. (C. 101, July 28, 1894; 12423, Apr. 19, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory negligence standard for line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: If apparent contributory negligence exists, the disability is still in the line of duty if the soldier used the reasonable degree of care and diligence which a person of ordinary prudence would exercise under the same circumstances; however, injuries caused by gross carelessness are not in line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule of ordinary prudence governs; gross carelessness may bar line-of-duty status, but many cases are left to individual determination on their merits. (C. 12370, Apr. 21, 1902; C. 2474, Aug. 3, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory acts short of culpable negligence may not bar benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some contributory acts may contribute to disability without reaching the degree of culpable contributory negligence that would preclude in-line status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts/authorities will often decline to lay down a strict rule and decide on the individual facts. (C. 2658, Oct. 15, 1896; Feb. 7, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Injuries in authorized athletic sports are in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Athletic sports properly indulged in by officers and enlisted men while in camp or garrison (and duly authorized contests away from reservation, e.g., return football games) are considered within the line of duty for resulting injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Athletics encouraged as part of military training; status depends on authorization and purpose (e.g., small-arms practice via hunting passes). (U. 24398, Feb. 13, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Confinement/arrest does not necessarily remove line-of-duty status
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier in arrest or confinement is not necessarily taken out of the line of duty; disabilities incurred while aiding the guard, while at authorized work, or as a result of confinement (e.g., rheumatism) may be in line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even deserters surrendered and killed while being conveyed have been held to die in line of duty in some circumstances. Investigation and context matter. (C. 2658, Oct. 15, 1890; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental conditions due to confinement may be in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Insanity or mental conditions that arise from confinement (even where confinement resulted from misconduct) have been held to be in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: insanity caused by brooding over confinement was treated as in line of duty rather than excluded because the confinement was due to misconduct. (G. 25809, Nov. 20, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Passes (short absences) generally preserve line-of-duty status
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pass' as incident to military service should not be for more than 24 hours and does not remove the soldier from the roster of 'present for duty'; generally, a man on pass is in line of duty, status being determined by duration and proximity to post rather than by the instrument's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hunting passes and similar privileges, intended as instruction/small-arms practice, fall within duty; characterization depends on duration and status created. (C. 15600, Dec. 10, 1903; 23666, Sept. 8, 1910; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized acts while on pass may negate line-of-duty status
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier on pass engages in an unauthorized act (e.g., intentionally discharging a borrowed rifle while bathing), resulting injury may not be considered incurred in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status depends on whether the act was authorized as incident to the pass. (C. 2658, Mar. 25, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Furloughs can be in line of duty when en route or complying with orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier on furlough may nevertheless be regarded as in line of duty in certain situations, such as while en route to a station or when complying with orders to report whereabouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function and compliance with orders during furlough may preserve in-line status. (C. 2658, Oct. 15, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pension-law term 'in the line of duty' construed liberally
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pension laws, the term 'in the line of duty' is broader than 'on duty' and is to be construed liberally and beneficially so as to advance entitlement rather than restrict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pension statutes being beneficial are given liberal construction; see multiple decisions. (R. 41, June 10, 1878; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross carelessness may bar pension entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross carelessness by a soldier that causes injury may render entitlement to a pension questionable on contributory-negligence grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate from ordinary contributory negligence rules; gross carelessness can defeat benefits. (C. 2474, Aug. 3, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infractions of discipline (fights/scuffles) not military duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts such as fighting or scuffling among soldiers are infractions of military discipline and are not considered performance of military duty; injuries from such acts are not in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two soldiers engaged in a scuffle leading to permanent injury — scuffle not performance of military duty. (Citation in text.)
